articles.description:
Ray on Emacs, Ray Zeitler writes about moving among windows
. It was a nostalgic moment for me because
other-window
Ctrl+x o) is that you may have to invoke it several times and, as Zeitler says, you can easily overshoot your target.


The next step in my journey—and apparently in Zeitler’s—was the discovery of Windmove. It allows you to use the arrow keys with (by default) the Shift key to move through the windows in a two-dimensional way. It’s a big improvement over the standard other-window command but it does interfere with certain Org bindings.


The next step in my journey was the discovery of abo-abo’s excellent ace-window package. It allows you to easily move among windows as well as perform many other actions such as splitting, deleting, moving, and copying windows. You can see a complete list at the link. To be honest, I use it almost exclusively for changing focus to another window. It works just like abo-abo’s other ace functions. You invoke it (I use Ctrl+x o to leverage my muscle memory) and the windows are labeled. Then you merely choose the label of the window to want to move to. As as added feature, if there are only two windows, it simply moves to the other window without the need for further input. You can also precede the command with the universal argument and it will swap the windows instead of simply moving to the target window.


All-in-all, ace-window is the best package I’ve found for window control. Perhaps it will be the next step on Zeitler’s journey too.
articles.title: Irreal: Moving Among Windows

  Recently I came across the windmove functions1.  This discovery
caused me to lose interest in bookmarks; now bookmarks are a mere
curiosity.



The windmove functions allow you to "operate" on a window; the
target window is given as a direction relative to point.
Operations include:


selection, like next-window, but direction overrides window order
deletion, like delete-window, but direction indicates the window
to delete
buffer display (not yet in use by the author)
S-<left>, S-<right>, 
S-<up>, S-<down> for window
selection.  For example, you can activate the window on the left with
windmove-left or S-<left>.



Org users already press S-<left>
(and S-<right>) on a heading to change TODO status.
As well, we press S-<up>
(and S-<down>) to increase (decrease) a heading's
priority.  Luckily, it's easy to specify a different modifier key.  I
configured my system to make windmove-dir respond to
M-s-<dir>2 with the following statement:



(windmove-default-keybindings '(meta super))

windmove-delete-left.  I've
defined C-M-s-<dir>3 for the
windmove-delete-dir functions by adding this to my init file:



(windmove-delete-default-keybindings '(control meta super))

other-window (C-x o), sometimes
"overshooting" the desired window, or I'd resort to using the mouse
to click in it.  Now with this intuitive method of selecting
windows, I can keep my hands on the keyboard and spend less time
figuring out how to get around.



Try it out!

articles.description:
The Art Of Not Asking Why reminds us of a very useful technique for iteratively searching through a series of files for those that contain a given set of terms. The process if simple but very flexible:


Open a Dired buffer with the files you want to search.
Use %g to do a regular expression search through the files for one of the terms. The files containing the term will be marked.
Use t to toggle the marks, resulting in all the files that don’t contain the term being marked.
Use k to temporarily hide the marked files, leaving only those that contain the term.
Go to step 2 using the next term.
A command to search through the contents of the marked files and show the results in another buffer.


The nice thing about this method is that it’s interactive: you progressively narrow down the list of target files by eliminating files that don’t contain the terms your looking for. You can, as JTR says, even manually eliminate files that you don’t want to consider as you go along. It’s a good technique and worth remembering.
articles.title: Irreal: Manual Dired Search

articles.description:
interesting little utility. Although it’s restricted to Safari and the Mac, it’s a nice idea that could probably be ported to other operating systems without difficulty. The idea is to be able to easily move from reading a Web page generated by Techinfo to reading the same information with the Emacs Info reader.


Reading Info pages with Emacs is straightforward and comfortable but the external utilities to read them outside of Emacs are terrible. Therefore, a lot us who started with another editor learned to go to the Web first rather than try to navigate the horrible external reader packages. But, as Choi points out, recent events have shown us that we can’t always count on the Web being there for us.


Choi’s solution to all this is the Counterpart utility that provides a menu in Safari to open the Web page’s content in Emacs. Of course, this only works for Techinfo generated content. Your immediate reaction may be, “Who cares?” but I’ve sometimes wished for something like this so that I could have the content side by side with whatever I was working on in Emacs. That also make’s it easy to copy text out of the Info buffer when you want to add a quote to whatever you’re writing.
articles.title: Irreal: Opening Techinfo Sourced Web Pages In Emacs

articles.description:
A year and a half ago I made a kitchen clock, which has worked well (except that I had to swap out the screen which broke mysteriously).
But yesterday I was having some work done here, so I had to remove one of the wifi access points here, and…  the clock stopped working.  *gasp*  Yes, because I had in my infinite wisdom decided that I would generate the clock face on a different machine, because the clock is a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, and I just assumed that it didn’t have enough memory to run Emacs (which I am, being a totally rational person, using to generate the SVG that’s being displayed).
So it’s a Rube Goldberguesque setup of having the image being generated on the main server, and then scp‘d over once a minute, and then being displayed on the console here in the kitchen.
But the wifi outage made me wonder — is it true that the machine doesn’t have enough memory to do it all on device?

So it’s got 416MB of useful memory, and while just running and doing nothing special, it’s using 129MB of that.
What happens if I load an Emacs with all the SVG libraries and stuff and generate the image?

It’s using 186MB — so the Emacs occupies about 50MB max.
*sigh*
It’s so easy to think of Emacs as this “big thing”, but everything has gotten so much bigger around it that it doesn’t matter at all any more.
So now I’ve changed the code to run on-device, so the only thing that goes AWOL if the wifi goes missing is updated temperatures.

Denote is a simple note-taking tool for Emacs.  It is based on the idea
that notes should follow a predictable and descriptive file-naming
scheme.  The file name must offer a clear indication of what the note is
about, without reference to any other metadata.  Denote basically
streamlines the creation of such files while providing facilities to
link between them.
Denote’s file-naming scheme is not limited to “notes”.  It can be used
for all types of file, including those that are not editable in Emacs,
such as videos.  Naming files in a consistent way makes their
filtering and retrieval considerably easier.  Denote provides relevant
facilities to rename files, regardless of file type.

articles.description:
As convenient as accessing online services can be, any disruption in availability without a fallback is painful. Given events of late, many are learning the hard way what it’s like to live without that fallback.
GNU Emacs has long supported reading documentation via the Info reader package. Info reader is a “local first” system, where all documentation is stored locally. The source format of the documentation is Texinfo which is exported to different formats, among them Info (used by the Emacs Info reader), HTML, and PDF.
Texinfo exported HTML is typically hosted on a website (usually GNU Project), with each Info node mapped to a URL path and indexed by most major search engine services.
Discovery of information in Texinfo documentation is frequently done via web search. If the user desires to view that Texinfo web page in the Emacs Info reader, that has to be done manually by corresponding the web page to its Info node.
Counterpart is a new utility to automate opening the Info node counterpart of a Texinfo exported web page in Emacs. This utility is designed for Emacs users on macOS who also use the Safari web browser. It requires the installation of a macOS Shortcut which is run from the main menu bar. More detail on using it can be found in the Counterpart User Guide.
Once a desired Info node is opened in Emacs, you can then bookmark it for later access, no internet connection required.
articles.title: Charles Choi: Opening Texinfo Web Pages in Emacs Info

huge fan of Journelly, which I use many times a day as my memo book. It has many other uses so take a look at the link if you’re interested in a note taking/journaling/private tweet/memo book application. I can’t recommend it enough.


Ramírez has, of course, done many other things, many or perhaps most, in the Emacs sphere. See his site for details. In a recent post he writes about making contributions to Emacs and getting them merged. Those of you who have been down that road know that it’s hard to get started. You have to navigate the GNU copyright assignment process, which seems needlessly baroque until you remember that all this is being run by volunteers.


You can follow the link to find out what his contributions are. They are all live in Emacs 31 so if you are up to date they are available to you now. The main takeaway for me was the satisfaction that Ramírez got from making those contributions. None of them were huge changes and merely scratched an itch that Ramírez had. If you have a small itch that you’ve scratched, you should consider sharing it with the community. You too can become part of Emacs’ long and influential history just as Hari Seldon’s successors in the Second Foundation contributed their own additions to Seldon’s Psychohistory.

articles.description:
made EWW his default browswer. That means that whenever he clicks on a URL and certain other links, the link is opened in EWW or—for special links—in another application that runs in Emacs. The point is, all browser activity starts in Emacs, usually in EWW.


Of course, Emacs can’t handle every browsing task so Blais uses the & key in EWW to escape to a “normal” browser. Blais says that EWW suffices for 85–90 percent of his use cases. He has some functions to kick off Emacs apps for MP4, PDF, and other specialized links. Everything else goes to EWW. He’s added a couple of custom bindings for EWW functions he uses a lot but it’s mostly a normal EWW instance.


Blais’ experiment shows that it is possible to almost browse from within Emacs. Sites that rely on JavaScript in an essential way are not going to work of course, and there are still a lot sites that insist on JavaScript so they can enforce the delivery of ads or implement a pay wall. Blais’ method gives us a chance to consider if those sites are worth viewing.
articles.title: Irreal: EWW As The Default Buffer

articles.description: This is the first of a few articles about the AI system I use for teaching maths. Basically, ten months ago I decided to buy an AI subscription to learn more about the technology, and today I run a small fleet of machines and agents that draft my lessons, check my exams, index my syllabus, and argue with me about design at midnight. This first article is about the recent years before any of that, because it turns out to be the part that made everything else possible.
articles.title: Matt Maguire: My AI Teaching Setup, Part 0: A Life in Plain Text

articles.description:
Part 2
 was about models and harnesses. But a model in a harness is still just a clever voice. What turned the setup into a system was the organs: the memory, the senses, and the reflexes bolted on around it. This is the final part, and it starts with a full circle.
The knowledge base that was already ten years old
People ask how I got my teaching knowledge into the AI. The answer is anticlimactic: I didn’t. I had spent a decade writing it in plain text — Org-mode notes, syllabus annotations, lesson reflections, the whole zettelkasten from Part 0
.
articles.title: Matt Maguire: My AI Teaching Setup, Part 3: The Organs

articles.description:
journey from Vim to Emacs. Actually, his journey was from Nano to Emacs by way of Vim. When he first started using Linux, Nano was the default editor and he began with that. Eventually he wanted more power and because Vim seemed more popular in the forums he inhabited, he learned Vim. He really like it and the power that it brought him was an eyeopener.


He experimented with other Vim-like implementations but they didn’t work for him so he stuck with Vim. Eventually he tried Emacs and almost immediately became a convert. Like me, he jumped right in and didn’t try to use Evil or some other Vim emulation. Like many of us, he loved the experience and now wants to do as much as he can in Emacs.


As always, a lot of the action is in the comments. Many said that immigrants from Vim should use Evil because it gives you the best of both worlds: the modal, composable editing commands of Vim and the power and flexibility of Emacs. Others said that Evil induces a sort of cognitive dissonance where neither system is fully in control.


There is, of course, the occasional post proclaiming loudly that Emacs is no good because it uses  Lisp with all those parentheses. The ankle biting aside, the comments offer an intelligent and useful commentary on Sahkopi4’s journey.
articles.title: Irreal: Vim To Emacs

articles.author: Ray Ratto
articles.description:
The Protect College Sports Act is a bad idea that seems stalled in Congress, and now we're finding out that the things most endangering college sports are coming from inside the house. In this case, the house in question is in Ann Arbor, Michigan, where ESPN's Pete Thamel reported that Trev Alberts, who was hired last week as the University of Michigan's athletic director, has now been un-hired for that role.
Yes, Alberts has apparently been fired before being hired as the Michigan AD, which may not quite be unprecedented but is inarguably damned weird. What made Michigan reverse course was that Alberts was the AD at Nebraska when Ashley Scoggin, a women's basketball player, sued the school in 2024 after being kicked off the team because of an alleged sexual relationship with assistant coach Chuck Love. Alberts was specifically named in the lawsuit for supporting the head coach's decision, not adequately addressing the assistant's misconduct, and, in a meeting with Scoggin's parents, supporting the decision to kick Scoggin off the team for dishonesty rather than dealing with the allegation of Love's misconduct. Alberts has denied those allegations in a court filing opposing the suit, but the baggage he would have brought to his new job, so soon after Michigan's issues with former football coach Sherrone Moore, seems to have given the school's administrators enough pause to bail on Alberts.
The sidebar here is that Alberts already signed a memorandum of understanding that he would be paid $17.2 million over the next five years. According to ESPN, Alberts' lawyer Tom Mars claimed that Alberts, who pronounced himself "shocked and disheartened" at the news, has not been given a reason for the school pulling out. Mars also maintained that there was no reference in the MOU to a background check. In other words, the fight isn't over the job but the money. Nothing says college sports quite like that last sentence.
articles.title: Michigan Pulls Offer On Incoming Athletic Director, Still Owes Him Money

articles.author: Patrick Redford
articles.description:
All of pop music can be thought of as existing on a temporal and stylistic continuum. Every up-and-coming artist is influenced to make music by the people they grew up listening to, and the truest marker of success is making music that's beloved enough to influence the next generation of musicians. In one sense, this is a straightforward description of the passage of time, but it's also the foundation of a complicated, fascinating legal space, where something like a particular yell can be thought of as proprietary. 
Which is all to say, I find the Taylor Swift–Olivia Rodrigo songwriting credit debate, the subject of this week's episode of Only If You Get Caught, extremely fascinating. Three songs on Rodrigo's 2021 debut album Sour, all of which was written by Rodrigo and her collaborator Dan Nigro, were the subjects of post-facto songwriting credit adjustments. Swift and her collaborators are now listed as the writers of two tracks, while two members of Paramore are listed as writers on one, despite none of them actually writing any of the material. How did something that strange happen? What does it say about the way intellectual property functions in music? Can someone own elements of a song?
We got into all that and more with the great Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding of Switched on Pop. This week's episode is the first in a three-episode, season-ending mini arc that we are calling Who Owns An Idea? The next episode is about IP theft in fashion, while the season finale is about AI.
articles.title: Solving The Olivia Rodrigo–Taylor Swift Songwriting Credit Debate Once And For All

This week's episode of Nothing But Respect marks the second straight week of interviewing the author of a landmark piece of sportswriting. This time, we were joined by James Herbert, who wrote a profile of longtime NBC investigative reporter and prolific NetsDaily blogger Bob Windrem for The Ringer, as well as longtime NBR favorite Ock Sportello, Nets fan and NetsDaily scholar. The descriptors "NBC investigative reporter" and "prolific NetsDaily blogger" both undersell Windrem. He was the first reporter to learn of Al Qaeda's role in 9/11; spent decades breaking extremely important, thorny international news stories; and also possesses perhaps the greatest corpus of knowledge on Nets of minor import, such as Sundiata Gaines, Cui Yongxi, and Milton Doyle. We spent a long time digging into the story.
You can find Nothing But Respect in Apple Podcasts or whatever podcast app you use. Follow the show on Instagram, and contact the Broke Jumper Tip Line at (347) 380-6426. Thanks for listening!

articles.author: Lauren Theisen
articles.description:
With under a minute to go, it looked like Washington had let the game slip through their fingers. The Cincinnati Bengals were behind 19-17 late, but they quickly got into kicking range. On second down, however, Joe Burrow lofted a pass right over the middle, and Commanders DB Rasul Douglas was in perfect position to make a clutch interception. Instead, the ball bounced off his hand, twice. To make matters worse, Douglas laid face-down on the ground in frustration after the near-pick, and the officials charged Washington with an injury timeout, their final one. They couldn't stop the clock after their third-down sack, which meant Evan McPherson's go-ahead kick passed through the uprights with only 46 seconds remaining.
Patrick Smith/Getty Images

That was all the time that Jayden Daniels needed. Coming off a game where he threw the winning touchdown in the final minute, the Commanders QB took advantage of a prevent defense to complete two long passes over the middle, setting up Drew Stevens for the winning 26-yard kick. For the first time since the 2024 playoffs, Washington has won back-to-back games.
articles.title: Jayden Daniels Has The Juice Again

The NWSL Players Association is concerned that Bay FC violated two different sections of the league’s collective bargaining agreement related to parental rights, according to PA Executive Director Meghann Burke. One of the sections is about non-discrimination, and one is about parental leave in the case that it overlaps with an expiring contract. The union is evaluating if there is enough information to file a grievance.
On Nov. 13, Bay announced its end-of-season roster updates. Three players who are new mothers—Caprice Dydasco, Abby Dahlkemper, and Emily Menges—were out of contract with the club and would not be re-signed. 
“On its face, we’re concerned there were three moms under contract with Bay who gave birth and were on maternity leave, and none of them are returning next season,” Burke told Defector. “Right away, that sort of raises an index of suspicion, where you try and understand what’s going on.”
articles.title: NWSL Players Association Has Concerns About Bay FC’s Treatment Of Players Who Have Taken Maternity Leave

He's back! He's back, he's back, he's freaking BACK! The Josh Johnson's Race Against Time Netflix series is surely just around the corner, and all Johnson needs to get it over is land one more gig before retirement so that he can become the first player to play for half the teams in his chosen sport.
We have visited the topic of Johnson's peripatetic journey through professional football before, with our first celebration dating all the way back to the dying embers of the COVID era. Johnson has come and gone as needed and as usual since, and the only reason to re-dredge this particular part of the bay is that Johnson started and finished Sunday's Arizona Cardinals game at Kansas City. It went about the way it should; the Cardinals are punting the season, and got punted in turn by the Chiefs, 34-7. Nobody seemed overly troubled by either the game play or the ensuing numbers, because nobody was under the illusion that this was an especially meaningful game.
That very much includes the Cardinals. They are uniquely awful because they are ritually awful; having to start four quarterbacks in four weeks is some deeply and unmistakably Cardinals Stuff. That they have reached the Josh Johnson stage of their season this early is fairly Cardinals as well, but less novel. There, at least, they have plenty of company.
articles.title: It’s Josh Johnson Time In The NFL

There’s a good chance you’ve heard of Tadich Grill, given that the restaurant is older than San Francisco itself. It’s existed in one form or another since 1849, when it opened under the name Coffee Stand. That was one year before the city of San Francisco was formally incorporated, and 118 years before the restaurant moved to its current location on California Street in the Financial District. Tadich has been doling out fresh seafood and mesquite-grilled slabs of meat to patrons through a lifespan that has included multiple earthquakes, two world wars, Prohibition and multiple pandemics. It’s not merely the oldest restaurant in San Francisco, but in all of California. An eternal landmark. I only needed to walk through its doors on an early evening this August to understand why.

articles.description:
My last psychiatrist was terrible.
Before every session, you fill out a form talking about how you’re feeling and so on as a way to evaluate whether or not your ADHD meds are working properly. For months, I’d invariably mention something about feeling pretty shitty about the political climate: ICE kidnapping people, trans folks having their very right to exist attacked, and so on.
In our session, she’d always ask me, without fail:
articles.title: Yes, I want to pay for that

articles.description:
Lately, I’ve been giving a lot of thought to what I would do if I wasn’t a web developer.
It’s not the first time I’ve thought about this, but the way AI is negatively affecting every aspect of our industry has pushed it top-of-mind again for me.
I’m not alone, either.
I posted about this in a handful of online communities I’m in, and so many developers are struggling with these same feelings.
articles.title: Life after coding

articles.description:
I saw this on one of the social sites the other day, but I can’t remember which (or who shared it)…
 “Wasting time” might be one of the strangest accusations we’ve ever invented. Apparently you can waste 2:00 p.m. by sitting under a tree doing nothing.
The afternoon was going to pass either way. The Earth was going to rotate either way. But because you didn’t convert those hours into money, errands or improvement, we decided the time itself was wasted.
articles.title: Wasting Time
